title: The Church as a body moved by the Word
source_text: Εἶτα ἐὰν μὲν τὴν αὐτὴν ἀρετὴν λέγοντες ἀνθρώπου καὶ θεοῦ οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Στοᾶς φιλόσοφοι μὴ εὐδαιμονέστερον λέγωσιν εἶναι τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν τοῦ ἐν ἀνθρώποις κατ᾿ αὐτοὺς σοφοῦ, ἀλλ᾿ ἴσην εἶναι τὴν ἀμφοτέρων εὐδαιμονίαν, Κέλσος οὐ καταγελᾷ οὐδὲ χλευάζει τὸ δόγμα· ἐὰν δ᾿ ὁ θεῖος λόγος φάσκῃ κολλᾶσθαι ὑπὸ τῆς ἀρετῆς καὶ ἑνοῦσθαι τῷ αὐτολόγῳ τὸν τέλειον, ὡς κατὰ τοῦτο ἀναβεβηκότας μὴ χωρίζειν ἡμᾶς τὴν Ἰησοῦ ψυχὴν τοῦ πρωτοτόκου „πάσης κτίσεως.“ γελᾷ τὸ λέγεσθαι υἱὸν θεοῦ Ἰησοῦν, οὐχ ὁρῶν, τίνα ἐστὶ τὰ περὶ αὐτοῦ ἐν ἀποῤῥήτῳ μυστικῶς ἐν ταῖς θείαις γραφαῖς λεγόμενα. ἵνα δὲ προσαγάγωμεν τῇ παραδοχῇ τοῦ λεγομένου τὸν βουλόμενον ἀκολουθίαις δογμάτων ἕπεσθαι καὶ ὠφελεῖσθαι, λέγομεν ὅτι σῶμα Χριστοῦ φασιν εἶναι οἱ θεῖοι λόγοι ὑπὸ τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ ψυχούμενον τὴν πᾶσαν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐκκλησίαν, μέλη δὲ τούτου τοῦ σώματος εἶναι ὡς ὅλου τούσδε τινὰς τοὺς πιστεύοντας· ἐπείπερ ὥσπερ ψυχὴ ζῳοποιεῖ καὶ κινεῖ τὸ σῶμα οὐ πεφυκὸς ἀφ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ κινεῖθαι ζωτικῶς. οὕτως ὁ λόγος κινῶν ἐπὶ τὰ δέοντα καὶ ἐνεργῶν τὸ ὅλον σῶμα τὴν ἐκκλησίαν κινεῖ καὶ ἕκαστον μέλος τῶν ἀπὸ τῆς ἐκκλησίας, οὐδὲν χωρὶς λόγου πράττοντα. εἴπερ οὖν τοῦτο οὐκ εὐκαταφρόνητον ὡς οἶμαι ἔχει ἀκολουθίαν, τί χαλεπὸν τῇ ἄκρᾳ καὶ ἀνυπερβλήτῳ κοινωνίᾳ πρὸς τὸν αὐτολόγον τὴν Ἰησοῦ ψυχὴν καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς τὸν Ἰησοῦν μὴ κεχωρίσθαι τοῦ μονογενοῦς καὶ πρωτοτόκου „πάσης κτίσεως“ μηδ᾿ ἕτερον ἔτι τυγχάνειν αὐτοῦ; ἀλλὰ ταῦτα μὲν ταύτῃ.
pass_a_gloss: Then if the philosophers from the Stoa (Στοά), saying the same virtue (ἀρετή) of man and of God, say that the God over all is not happier (εὐδαιμονέστερος) than the wise one (σοφός) among men according to them, but that the happiness (εὐδαιμονία) of both is equal (ἴσος), Celsus does not laugh down (καταγελάω) nor mock (χλευάζω) the doctrine (δόγμα); but if the divine word says that the perfect one is cleaved (κολλάομαι) by virtue and united (ἑνόω) to the Word-itself (αὐτόλογος), so that in this respect, we having ascended (ἀναβαίνω), we do not separate the soul of Jesus from the firstborn 'of all creation', he laughs at Jesus being called son of God, not seeing what are the things about him said in secret (ἐν ἀπορρήτῳ) mystically (μυστικῶς) in the divine writings (γραφαί). In order to bring (προσάγω) to the acceptance (παραδοχή) of what is said the one wishing to follow (ἕπομαι) the sequences (ἀκολουθίαι) of doctrines and be benefited (ὠφελέω), we say that the divine words say that the body (σῶμα) of Christ, ensouled (ψυχόω) by the son of God, is the whole church (ἐκκλησία) of God, and members (μέλη) of this body, as of a whole (ὅλον), are these particular believers (οἱ πιστεύοντες); since just as a soul makes alive (ζῳοποιέω) and moves (κινέω) the body, not being of a nature (φύω) to be moved of itself vitally (ζωτικῶς), so the Word, moving to the things needful (τὰ δέοντα) and working (ἐνεργέω) the whole body, moves the church and each member of those from the church, doing nothing apart from Word/reason (χωρὶς λόγου). If then this has, as I think, a not easily despised (εὐκαταφρόνητος) sequence, what is difficult (χαλεπός), by the highest and unsurpassable (ἀνυπέρβλητος) communion (κοινωνία) with the Word-itself, for the soul of Jesus and, simply (ἁπαξαπλῶς), Jesus not to have been separated from the only-begotten (μονογενής) and firstborn 'of all creation', nor any longer to be other (ἕτερος) than him? But these things thus.
pass_b_english: Further, if the philosophers of the Stoa, who say that the virtue of man and of God is the same, say that the God who is over all is no happier than the one they count wise among men, but that the happiness of both is equal, Celsus does not laugh at the doctrine or mock it. But if the divine word says that the perfect man is joined and united by virtue to the Word himself, so that, rising by this line of reasoning, we do not separate the soul of Jesus from the firstborn “of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), he laughs at Jesus’ being called Son of God, not seeing what it is that the divine Scriptures say of him in secret and in a mystery.

In order to bring anyone who wishes to follow the sequence of doctrines and to profit by it to accept what is said, we say this. The divine words say that the whole Church of God is the body of Christ, given its soul by the Son of God, and that individual believers are members of this body, taken as a whole (1 Corinthians 12:27; Ephesians 1:22–23). For just as the soul gives life to the body and moves it, though the body is not by nature able to move itself with the motion of life, so the Word, moving the whole body, the Church, to what is needful and working in it, moves it and each member of those who belong to the Church; and they do nothing apart from the Word.

If, then, this has a coherence not to be lightly despised, as I think it has, what difficulty is there in holding that the soul of Jesus, or in a word Jesus himself, by that highest and unsurpassable communion with the Word himself, has not been separated from the only-begotten and firstborn “of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), and is no longer other than he? But enough of this here.

choices.choice: The Stoic claim is that God and the wise man have the same virtue and equal happiness; Origen gives no specific text, so no source is cited. ‘The divine word’ (ὁ θεῖος λόγος) here means Scripture’s teaching, so ‘word’ is lowercase; ‘the Word himself’ (αὐτόλογος) is Christ. The body-of-Christ teaching is a summary, not a quotation: 1 Corinthians 12:27 and Ephesians 1:22-23 are given as its clearest sources. ‘They do nothing apart from the Word’: the Greek participle (πράττοντα) agrees with ‘each member’, and χωρὶς λόγου also carries the sense ‘without reason’; the play on λόγος cannot be kept in English. Source misprint κινεῖθαι for κινεῖσθαι. ‘Only-begotten’ (μονογενής) echoes John 1:14, 18; left uncited inline as a title. ‘The whole body, the Church’ keeps the Greek apposition τὸ ὅλον σῶμα τὴν ἐκκλησίαν as the object of the Word’s moving.

'He does not see what is said of him ... hidden and in a mystery' -> participle kept: 'not seeing what it is that the divine Scriptures say of him in secret and in a mystery' (τίνα ἐστὶ ... ἐν ἀποῤῥήτῳ μυστικῶς)
Purpose clause put in English order: 'In order to bring anyone who wishes ... to accept what is said'; ὠφελεῖσθαι 'to profit by it'
'believers, one by one' -> 'individual believers' (τούσδε τινὰς τοὺς πιστεύοντας)
Word-and-body sentence follows the Greek apposition: the Word moves 'the whole body, the Church' and each member (old version moved 'the whole body' and then 'the Church' as if two objects)
'and indeed Jesus himself' -> 'or in a word Jesus himself' (ἁπαξαπλῶς); 'nor is any longer other' -> 'and is no longer other' (μηδ᾿ ἕτερον ἔτι)
Colossians 1:15, 1 Corinthians 12:27 and Ephesians 1:22-23 checked; the body-of-Christ citations are summary allusions and fit
